timeline.title: Chronology of Harappan Glyptic Art
timeline.description: Historical development of carving seals in the Indus Valley Civilization.

cards.details: Emergence of square and button-shaped seals. Primarily made of terracotta or soft stone. Simple geometric designs or basic animal markings.

Apex of glyptic art. Mass production of square steatite seals with standardized motifs (Unicorn, Pashupati) and short picto-phonetic inscriptions. Cylindrical seals reveal trade contacts with Mesopotamia.
Decline of centralized cities. Decline in seal quality, disappearance of animal iconography, and loss of written inscriptions.

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps
items: Trap 1: The Horse Depiction: While bulls, tigers, rhinos, and elephants are widely depicted, no horse is represented on any Harappan seal. Any option listing a horse as a seal motif is an exam trap.
Trap 2: Decipherment of Inscriptions: The pictographic script on seals remains completely undeciphered. Statements claiming we know the names of kings or merchants written on seals are false.
Trap 3: Direction of Writing: The script on the seals was typically written from right to left (boustrophedon style). However, when pressed onto clay, the impressions read left to right.
Trap 4: Absence of Cow: Despite the abundance of humped bulls, cows are never depicted on Harappan seals.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Explore the artistic, technical, and socio-economic dimensions of Harappan seals.

sections.title: 1. Material Composition & Typology of Seals
sections.content:
Seals represent the most artistic and technologically standardized artifacts of the Indus Valley Civilization. They were produced in specialized craft centers and served as hallmarks of Harappan urban identity.

Materials and Techniques
  • Steatite (Soapstone): Over 90% of seals are made of steatite. It was carved easily and then fired to high temperatures (c. 1000°C) to whiten and harden it into enstatite.
  • Other Materials: Agate, chert, jasper, copper, silver, gold, faience, and terracotta were also used.
  • Shapes: Square seals (with a pierced boss/loop on the back) are standard. Rectangular seals (usually containing only text) and circular button seals are also found.
Script & Writing Direction
  • Pictographic Script: The script contains about 400 signs, showing logo-syllabic symbols representing words or syllables.
  • Direction: Written from right to left in a single line, or alternating (boustrophedon) for multi-line texts.
  • Average Length: Most seals carry 5 to 6 signs. The longest inscription contains 26 signs.

Comparative Matrix of Major Seal Categories:

Seal Type Primary Site Key Animal / Iconography Material Used Function / Significance
Pashupati Seal Mohenjo-daro Seated deity, Elephant, Tiger, Rhino, Buffalo, 2 Deer Steatite (Soapstone) Religious/Ritualistic; represents proto-Shiva or animistic deity.
Unicorn Seal Found across all major sites One-horned mythical animal with a manger/stand Steatite (most common) Most common commercial seal; likely represents merchant guild or elite clan badge.
Copper Tablets Harappa & Mohenjo-daro Inscriptions on one side, animals/deities on other Copper plates Identification tokens, amulets, or currency/license.
Terracotta Sealings Lothal (dense warehouse hoard) Seal impressions on clay, cloth fiber impressions on back Fired clay / Terracotta Trade logistics; verified cargo contents and merchant identity during transit.

sections.title: 2. Iconography: Pashupati and Mythical Beasts
sections.content:
The iconography of seals offers invaluable insights into the religious beliefs, mythology, and social structures of the Harappans.

The Pashupati Seal
  • Deity: A three-horned seated figure in a yogic posture (Mulabandhasana) on a low throne. Often identified by John Marshall as 'Proto-Shiva'.
  • Animals: Surrounded by four wild animals: Tiger and Elephant on the right; Rhinoceros and Buffalo on the left.
  • Throne Base: Two antelopes or deer are depicted directly under the seat.
The Unicorn & Nature Symbolism
  • The Unicorn Motif: A one-horned mythical bull-like creature (the most popular motif). Usually stands in front of a cylindrical 'sacred stand' or filter/incense burner.
  • Nature Worship: Seals showing a deity inside a Peepal tree with a worshipper and a sacrificial goat suggest animistic rituals.

sections.title: 3. Socio-Economic Functions & Trade Logistics
sections.content:
Beyond art, seals were essential instruments of state authority, guild identification, and trade control in a sprawling maritime and terrestrial commercial network.

Commercial Sealing and Security
  • Warehouse Logistics: Knots on cargo sacks were covered in wet clay, and seals were pressed into them. Once dried, these sealings proved that the contents had not been opened or tampered with.
  • Findspots: Lothal's warehouse yielded over 90 clay sealings, proving its role as an active port.
Administrative and Personal Use
  • Merchant Badges: Used as identity cards or passports by travelling merchants.
  • Amulets: The pierced boss on the back allowed them to be worn on strings around the neck or wrist to ward off evil.
  • Cylindrical Seals: Found in small numbers, indicating trade connections with Mesopotamia (where cylindrical seals were standard).

mockTestQuestions.q:
With reference to the Indus Valley Civilization seals, consider the following statements:
1. The Pashupati Seal represents a three-horned seated deity surrounded by five animals under the throne.
2. The unicorn is the most common animal motif represented on square seals.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because the deity is surrounded by four animals (tiger, elephant, rhino, buffalo) and has two deer *under* the throne. Statement 2 is correct; the unicorn is the most popular motif.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following animals is NOT depicted on any Harappan seals?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The horse is completely absent from all Harappan seals.

mockTestQuestions.q: The majority of Harappan seals were made of steatite (soapstone). What was the main reason for this choice of material?
opts: It was imported from Mesopotamia at low cost.
It is a soft stone that can be carved easily and hardens upon firing.
It was the only stone available in the Indus plain.
It had magnetic properties used for alignment.
mockTestQuestions.sol: Steatite is extremely soft and easy to carve with copper tools, but turns into very hard enstatite when fired.

mockTestQuestions.q: With reference to the writing on Harappan seals, which of the following is correct?
opts: The script was written from left to right in all cases.
The writing represents a fully deciphered Sanskrit script.
The average inscription contains 5 to 6 signs.
The longest inscription has exactly 100 signs.
mockTestQuestions.sol: The script is undeciphered, usually written from right to left, and the average inscription length is 5 to 6 characters.

mockTestQuestions.q: The discovery of cylindrical seals in Harappan sites is an indicator of trade links with which region?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Cylindrical seals were typical of Mesopotamia; their discovery in Harappan cities confirms maritime trade.

mockTestQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Terracotta sealings were used as coins for commercial transactions.
2. Clay sealings with cloth impressions prove that Harappans exported textiles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because sealings were trade tags, not coins. Statement 2 is correct; cloth fiber impressions on the back of sealings prove trade in packaged textiles.

mockTestQuestions.q: The 'Pashupati Seal' was discovered at which of the following archaeological sites?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Pashupati Seal was discovered at Mohenjo-daro.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the 'boustrophedon' style of writing observed on some multi-line seals?
opts: Writing vertically from top to bottom
Writing in alternating directions (right to left, then left to right)
Writing in circular spirals from the center outwards
mockTestQuestions.sol: Boustrophedon writing alternates direction in successive lines (like an ox plowing a field).

mockTestQuestions.q: The 'boss' (loop) on the reverse side of a square steatite seal served what primary purpose?
opts: It acted as a handle for pressing the seal and allowed a suspension cord to pass through.
It was used to measure weight in gold.
It served as a key to lock boxes.
It indicated the value of the merchant guild.
mockTestQuestions.sol: The boss or loop was used to hold the seal during stamping and to pass a thread through so it could be worn as an amulet.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following deities/trees is most commonly depicted on Harappan seals representing nature worship?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Peepal tree (Ficus religiosa) is the most commonly depicted sacred tree in Harappan seal art.
